title: April Deal: Quick Resolution
description: Trump's April 6 energy-strike deadline works as intended: facing the prospect of systematic destruction of Iran's oil infrastructure (Kharg Island terminal, refineries, export pipelines), Iran's fragmented post-Khamenei leadership — likely an IRGC-Guardian Council coalition acting as interim authority — accepts modified terms that allow both sides to claim partial victory. The deal framework involves: Iran accepts comprehensive IAEA inspection of all nuclear sites including military dimensions; the US agrees to a phased sanctions relief timeline and implicit regime survival guarantees; Hormuz reopens under international naval escort within weeks. Turkey and Qatar serve as co-guarantors. The Houthi and Hezbollah dimensions are managed through a separate de-escalation annex brokered by Saudi Arabia (Houthis) and France (Hezbollah/Lebanon). This scenario requires Iran's leadership to prioritize regime survival over ideological resistance — a calculation the IRGC's institutional interests (preserving its economic empire) may drive even if clerical hardliners resist. Trump frames the outcome as 'the greatest deal in history' — nuclear program destroyed, favorable terms extracted, American casualties minimal. The critical vulnerability is durability: a deal negotiated under extreme duress, with a fragmented Iranian counterpart, and without congressional treaty ratification may collapse within 2-3 years — the JCPOA precedent where the next administration abandoned the framework.

title: Negotiated Settlement by Summer
description: The April 6 deadline passes without Iranian acceptance, triggering US energy infrastructure strikes that devastate Iran's oil export capacity but do not produce capitulation. Instead, the conflict enters a grinding 2-4 month phase of continued US air operations, Iranian proxy activation (Hezbollah maintaining pressure on Israel, Houthis disrupting Red Sea shipping), and mounting economic costs on all sides. The settlement emerges through a convergence of pressures by June-August 2026: Turkey and China co-mediate, leveraging Turkey's NATO membership and Iran relationship, and China's economic leverage over both Iranian reconstruction needs and global oil market stability. The framework involves face-saving elements for both sides: Iran agrees to 'voluntary' nuclear transparency measures (not framed as imposed terms); the US accepts a phased withdrawal of additional forces deployed for the conflict; sanctions relief is tied to a multi-year verification schedule; Hormuz reopens under a multilateral naval monitoring arrangement. The Houthi/Hezbollah situation is addressed through parallel tracks — Saudi Arabia negotiates a Yemen ceasefire extension, Israel and Hezbollah agree to an enhanced UNIFIL framework. This is the JCPOA negotiation model compressed into months rather than years, driven by the urgency of active conflict rather than the patience of peacetime diplomacy. The deal is more durable than the April scenario because it involves broader international buy-in, but it comes at the cost of months of additional destruction, thousands of casualties, and a global economic shock from sustained Hormuz closure.

title: Frozen Conflict
description: No ceasefire materializes. The April 6 deadline passes, the US strikes energy infrastructure, Iran absorbs the damage and refuses to capitulate, and the conflict enters an indefinite low-intensity phase. Active large-scale US air operations wind down after 3-5 months as high-value target sets are exhausted, but no formal cessation occurs. Iran's proxy network maintains periodic harassment operations: Hezbollah conducts low-level border attacks on Israel, Houthis continue Red Sea disruption, Iraqi militias periodically target US bases. The US maintains an enhanced CENTCOM posture and naval presence but shifts from active combat to containment. Hormuz partially reopens under US Navy escort — commercial shipping at reduced volumes with war-risk insurance premiums — but never returns to pre-war normalcy. Iran's post-Khamenei power structure consolidates around an IRGC-dominated military government that uses the 'survival against American aggression' narrative for domestic legitimacy, analogous to Saddam's post-1991 positioning. Nuclear verification is impossible — the IAEA has no access, and Iran's reconstitution efforts proceed in dispersed, hardened facilities. This is the Korea/Kashmir model: fighting stops without resolution, underlying conflict persists indefinitely, and the region lives with permanent tension. The economic costs are sustained: oil markets price in a permanent $15-30/barrel risk premium, global trade routes remain disrupted, and the $200-500 billion war cost is compounded by ongoing containment expenses. RAND's analysis of asymmetric wars shows that this 'no resolution' outcome occurs in the majority of cases — formal resolution within 5 years is the historical exception.

title: Wider Regional War
description: The Houthi entry into the war and Hezbollah's active operations against Israel prove to be not peripheral developments but the leading edge of a full regional conflagration. The escalation cascade follows a specific sequence: (1) Houthi anti-ship missiles strike a major commercial vessel or US warship in the Red Sea, killing dozens and triggering US strikes on Houthi leadership and infrastructure in Yemen; (2) Hezbollah intensifies rocket attacks on northern Israel, prompting an Israeli ground incursion into southern Lebanon; (3) Iraqi Shia militias, now openly coordinated with IRGC remnants, attack US bases in Iraq with sophisticated Iranian-supplied weapons, producing US casualties; (4) Saudi Arabia, facing Houthi ballistic missile strikes on Aramco infrastructure (repeating the 2019 attack at larger scale), requests US intervention or conducts its own strikes; (5) the conflict becomes a simultaneous five-theater war — Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq, and the Gulf — exceeding US military and diplomatic bandwidth. Iran's strategy in this scenario is rational: having lost the conventional air war, the IRGC activates its primary remaining asymmetric asset — the proxy network — to impose costs that make continued US operations politically unsustainable. The nuclear escalation risk rises: Iran may activate undisclosed enrichment sites or move toward weaponization threshold as a deterrent against regime change. Russia increases intelligence sharing and advanced air defense resupply; China shifts from strategic ambiguity toward overt economic support for Iran. Congressional authorization becomes a constitutional crisis as the War Powers clock expires. CFR estimates 100,000-500,000 casualties across all parties within the first year, with refugee flows exceeding 10 million.
